subject: Computer Science
titleHi: ई-कॉमर्स, MIS एवं व्यवसाय में IT
summary: Covers e-commerce types, business and revenue models, electronic payment systems, security and EDI; information systems for management (TPS, MIS, DSS, ESS, expert systems, data warehousing and OLAP); knowledge management; and ERP with related business systems such as CRM, SCM and accounting software. DSSSB questions are mostly conceptual: model classification, payment-system features, system components and types of knowledge.

sections.heading: E-commerce and e-business: basics
sections.body:
**E-commerce** is buying and selling goods, services and information over electronic networks, mainly the Internet. **E-business** is broader: using Internet technology for all business processes - buying and selling plus serving customers, collaborating with partners, internal operations and supply chains. Every e-commerce activity is e-business, not vice versa.

**Benefits**: global reach, 24×7 availability, lower transaction and inventory costs, personalisation, faster delivery of information, reduced paperwork. **Limitations**: security and privacy concerns, lack of trust, inability to touch products, dependence on infrastructure, legal and tax issues.

**Key drivers of e-business** include commercial benefits (cost reduction, new markets), the requirements of customers and suppliers, a skilled and committed workforce, and available technology. **Barriers** may be internal (cost, lack of in-house experts, unclear business model, organisational culture) or external, such as **Internet infrastructure**, security, legal frameworks and customer readiness.

**Fulfilment**: delivery of goods ordered from an e-shop depends on the size, nature and urgency of the products and on the delivery location - not on the product's cost. Visibility of an e-commerce website is improved by a sensible, easily guessed domain name, fresh content (special offers, eye-catching information), **SEO** (search engine optimisation), paid search (SEM), social media and email marketing.

sections.heading: E-commerce business and revenue models
sections.body:
A **business model** describes how a firm creates value and earns revenue. One textbook classification, used in DSSSB questions, divides Internet business models into two groups:
- **Transplanted real-world business models** - existing models moved online: mail-order, advertising-based, **subscription**, **free trial**, direct marketing, real estate, incentive schemes, B2B, and combinations.
- **Native Internet business models** - born on the Internet: **library** model, **freeware** model, information barter, **digital products and digital delivery**, **access provision** (ISPs), website hosting and other Internet services.

Common **revenue models**: advertising, subscription, transaction fee/commission, sales of goods, affiliate (referral commission), freemium (basic free, premium paid). Other web models: **brokerage/marketplace** (brings buyers and sellers together), **merchant** (e-tailer), **manufacturer direct**, **infomediary** (sells collected information), **community** (social networks).

**M-commerce** (mobile commerce) reduces transaction costs by streamlining processes and enables mobile coupons, location-based services and mobile payments; **mobile security** remains one of its main impediments, along with small screens and connectivity.

sections.heading: Electronic payment systems
sections.body:
An **Electronic Payment System (EPS)** transfers money electronically. Types:
- **Credit card** (pay later, a credit limit) and **debit card** (pay now from a bank account); processed through a **payment gateway** that authorises the transaction.
- **Smart card** - plastic card with an embedded microchip storing data/value; contact or contactless.
- **E-wallet / digital wallet** - stores money or card details on a phone or online; **e-cash** (digital cash), **e-cheque**.
- **Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT)**: **NEFT** (National Electronic Funds Transfer - transfers settled in batches on a deferred net basis; no minimum amount; now available round the clock), **RTGS** (Real Time Gross Settlement - each transaction settled individually and immediately; meant for large values, minimum ₹2 lakh), **IMPS** (Immediate Payment Service, instant 24×7, run by NPCI) and **UPI** (Unified Payments Interface, NPCI, uses a virtual payment address and mobile app).
- Net banking, cash on delivery.

**NEFT advantages** include legal backing for transactions, round-the-clock availability, near-real-time credit with secure settlement, positive confirmation to the remitter (SMS/e-mail) and no need to visit a branch.

**Online share trading** steps: open a **Demat account** and an online trading account, transfer funds from the bank to the trading account, place the order; once confirmed it is executed on the exchange and shares are credited to the Demat account.

sections.heading: E-commerce security and EDI
sections.body:
Security requirements: **confidentiality**, **integrity**, **authentication**, **non-repudiation**, **availability**.
- **SSL/TLS** (Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security) encrypts data between browser and server (`https`, port 443). It requires a **server certificate**, uses a dedicated TCP/IP socket, and operates **above the transport layer** (between TCP and the application layer) - not between the network and transport layers.
- **SET** (Secure Electronic Transaction) - card-payment protocol from Visa and MasterCard using dual signatures; historically important, little used now.
- **Digital signatures** and **PKI** (Public Key Infrastructure, digital certificates issued by a Certifying Authority) provide authentication and non-repudiation.
- **Two-factor authentication / OTP**, encryption, firewalls, and the PCI-DSS standard for card data.

**EDI (Electronic Data Interchange)** is the computer-to-computer exchange of standard business documents (purchase orders, invoices) in a machine-readable format between businesses, often over **VANs** (Value Added Networks). Standards: **ANSI X12** (US standard for EDI) and **UN/EDIFACT** (international). EDI reduces paperwork, errors and cycle time; it is an early form of B2B e-commerce.

sections.heading: Management Information System (MIS)
sections.body:
An **information system** collects, processes, stores and distributes information to support decisions and control. **MIS** provides managers with regular, structured reports (scheduled, exception, demand and summary reports) drawn mainly from internal transaction data to support planning and control, mainly at the **middle management** level.

**Resources / components of MIS**: **hardware, software, people, data** and **procedures** (plus networks). Typical components include databases (internal and **external databases**), data entry, processing, reporting and inquiry. Examples: railway reservation, electronic banking operations with a payment gateway, and logistics applications that streamline transport are all information systems that support management.

**Types of information systems by management level**:
- **TPS (Transaction Processing System)** - operational level; records, processes, validates and stores day-to-day transactions (payroll, order entry, billing, reservation) for later retrieval and use. **OLTP** (On-Line Transaction Processing) gives immediate responses, keeps the database always up to date and uses resources efficiently.
- **MIS** - middle management; routine summary reports.
- **DSS (Decision Support System)** - middle/senior managers; semi-structured decisions, what-if analysis.
- **ESS/EIS (Executive Support/Information System)** - top management; strategic, unstructured decisions using internal and external data, dashboards with drill-down.
- **OAS** (Office Automation) and **KWS** (Knowledge Work Systems) support clerical and knowledge workers.

Decision types (Simon): **structured** (routine, programmable), **semi-structured**, **unstructured** (novel, judgement-based). Simon's decision process: intelligence → design → choice (→ implementation).

sections.heading: Decision Support Systems and Expert Systems
sections.body:
**DSS** is an interactive, computer-based system that helps managers solve **semi-structured** problems using data and models. Components:
- **Data management subsystem** - database (internal and external data).
- **Model management subsystem** - model base (statistical, financial, optimisation models).
- **User interface (dialogue) subsystem**.
- **Knowledge-based (knowledge engine) subsystem** in intelligent DSS.
A **Group DSS** supports group decision making.

**Expert System (ES)** - an AI program that captures the knowledge of human experts in a **narrow domain** to give advice. Components: **knowledge base** (facts and IF-THEN rules), **inference engine** (applies rules; **forward chaining** is data-driven, **backward chaining** is goal-driven), user interface, **explanation facility** and knowledge acquisition facility. The **knowledge engineer** acts as the intermediary between the domain expert (specialist) and the expert system. Classic examples: MYCIN (medical diagnosis), DENDRAL (chemical analysis).

sections.heading: Data warehouse, OLAP and business intelligence
sections.body:
A **data warehouse** is a relational database designed for **query and analysis** rather than transaction processing. Inmon's definition: **subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile** collection of data supporting management decisions. Data is loaded through **ETL** (Extract, Transform, Load); a **data mart** is a departmental subset.

**OLAP** (On-Line Analytical Processing) analyses multidimensional data (cubes): **roll-up** (summarise), **drill-down** (more detail), **slice** (fix one dimension), **dice** (sub-cube), **pivot** (rotate view).

**Data mining** discovers hidden patterns: classification, clustering, **association rules** (market-basket analysis), regression/prediction, anomaly detection. **Business intelligence (BI)** = tools and processes (reports, dashboards, OLAP, mining) turning data into decisions. **Exploratory data analysis** in big-data analytics offers flexible ways to generate hypotheses.

sections.heading: Knowledge management
sections.body:
**Knowledge management (KM)** is the process of identifying, creating, organising, storing and disseminating (sharing) information and expertise within an organisation so that it can be reused. Hierarchy: **data** (raw facts) → **information** (processed data) → **knowledge** (information with context and experience) → wisdom.

**Types of knowledge**:
- **Tacit knowledge** - highly personal, based on experience and skill, **hard to formalise** and communicate (e.g. how a senior teacher handles a difficult class).
- **Explicit knowledge** - codified and captured in documents such as manuals, reports, guides and databases, so it can be easily shared.

**SECI model** (Nonaka and Takeuchi) - knowledge conversion: **Socialisation** (tacit → tacit, by shared experience), **Externalisation** (tacit → explicit, writing it down), **Combination** (explicit → explicit, merging documents), **Internalisation** (explicit → tacit, learning by doing).

**Key KM processes**: knowledge gathering/capture → storage and organisation → distribution/sharing → use/application. KM is often described along the dimensions of **people, process and technology**, and of **strategy and content**.

**KM systems (KMS)**: knowledge repositories, document management, intranets and portals, wikis, expert directories, communities of practice, lessons-learned databases. Building a KMS is a continuous, people-centred effort with strong human and cultural implications, not a cheap one-time technical installation. A **Chief Knowledge Officer (CKO)** may lead KM.

sections.heading: ERP and integrated business systems
sections.body:
**ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning)** is an integrated software suite in which all business functions share **one common database**, so data is entered once and is available in real time across departments. Typical **modules**: finance and accounting, human resources (payroll), production planning/manufacturing, materials management and inventory, sales and distribution, purchasing, plus extensions for SCM and CRM. Major vendors: SAP, Oracle, Microsoft Dynamics.

**Benefits**: integration and a single source of truth, standardised processes, better reporting and decisions, reduced duplication. **Challenges**: high cost, long implementation, customisation difficulty, resistance to change, need for training. Implementation approaches: **big-bang** (all modules at once) or **phased**.

**Related systems**:
- **BPR (Business Process Re-engineering)** - fundamental rethinking and radical redesign of business processes (Hammer and Champy), often done with ERP adoption.
- **CRM (Customer Relationship Management)** - operational (sales and service automation), analytical (customer data analysis) and collaborative CRM.
- **SCM (Supply Chain Management)** - managing flows from suppliers through manufacturing to customers: plan, source, make, deliver, return.
- **Accounting software** - e.g. **Tally**, widely used by Indian businesses for accounts, inventory and GST.
- **Project management software** (e.g. MS Project) - project planning, scheduling, resource allocation, task lists and team communication.
- **HRMS**, point-of-sale (POS) systems and office suites support other business functions.

workedExamples.problem: Classify: (a) a student sells an old cycle to another student on a classifieds website; (b) a car maker orders tyres from its supplier's portal; (c) a citizen downloads a birth certificate from a municipal portal; (d) a shopper buys a phone from an online store using a mobile app.
workedExamples.solution:
(a) **C2C** - both parties are consumers; the website is only the platform.
(b) **B2B** - business buying from business (could also use EDI).
(c) **G2C** - government service to a citizen.
(d) **B2C**, and because a mobile device is used it is also **m-commerce**.

workedExamples.problem: Which information system fits each need? (a) recording every ticket booked at a counter; (b) a monthly report of branch-wise sales for regional managers; (c) a what-if model of profit if prices are cut by 5%; (d) a dashboard of company KPIs and competitor news for the CEO; (e) a program that asks a farmer questions and suggests a crop disease.
workedExamples.solution:
(a) **TPS** - routine transaction recording at the operational level (OLTP).
(b) **MIS** - scheduled, structured summary report for middle management.
(c) **DSS** - model-based what-if analysis for a semi-structured decision.
(d) **ESS/EIS** - strategic summary with external data for top management.
(e) **Expert system** - narrow domain, machine questions the user, inference engine gives advice.

workedExamples.problem: Identify the SECI mode: (a) a new teacher sits in a senior's class and picks up her style; (b) the senior writes a guide on handling noisy classes; (c) the school combines several guides into one handbook; (d) the new teacher practises the handbook techniques until they become natural.

Practice: An online store had 40,000 visitors in a month; 3,200 carts were created and 800 orders completed, with total sales of ₹12,00,000. Find the conversion rate, cart abandonment rate and average order value.

Choose a suitable payment method: (a) a company pays ₹50 lakh to a supplier and wants immediate, individual settlement; (b) a person sends ₹500 to a friend instantly through a phone using a virtual payment address; (c) a small transfer where batch settlement is acceptable.
workedExamples.solution:
(a) **RTGS** - real-time gross settlement, meant for large values (minimum ₹2 lakh), settled individually.
(b) **UPI** - instant transfer using a virtual payment address on a mobile app (built on NPCI's instant payment infrastructure).
(c) **NEFT** - batch-wise deferred net settlement with no minimum amount.

pitfalls: E-business is broader than e-commerce; all e-commerce is e-business, not the reverse.
Subscription and free-trial models are transplanted real-world models; library, freeware, digital products and access provision are native Internet models.
RTGS = gross, individual, real-time; NEFT = deferred net settlement in batches.
SSL/TLS works above the transport layer, not between network and transport layers.
ANSI X12 is the EDI standard (not X.25 or X.75, which are network standards).
TPS records and validates transactions; DSS supports semi-structured decisions; ESS is for top management.
In an expert system the machine queries the user; in a DSS the user queries the machine.
The knowledge engineer, not the inference engine, is the intermediary between the expert and the system.
Tacit knowledge is personal and hard to formalise; explicit knowledge is documented.
Data warehouse is non-volatile and time-variant; it is for analysis (OLAP), not transactions (OLTP).

UPI and IMPS are run by NPCI.
